{{History of Japan}}

The '''Meiji Restoration''' ({{lang-ja|明治維新|Meiji Ishin}}), referred to at the time as the {{Nihongo|'''Honorable Restoration'''|御維新|Goisshin}}, and also known as the '''Meiji Renovation''', '''Revolution''', '''Regeneration''', '''Reform''', or '''Renewal''', was a political event that restored practical imperial rule to Japan in 1868 under {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}}. Although there were ruling emperors before the Meiji Restoration, the events restored practical abilities and consolidated the political system under the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor of Japan|1=Emperor of Japan}}.{{ref|a}} The goals of the restored government were expressed by the new emperor in the {{ill|Charter Oath|en|Charter Oath|WD=Q702056|lt=Charter Oath|1=Charter Oath}}

The Restoration led to enormous changes in Japan's political and social structure and spanned both the late {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} (often called the {{ill|Bakumatsu|en|Bakumatsu|WD=Q804558|lt=Bakumatsu|1=Bakumatsu}}) and the beginning of the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], during which time Japan rapidly {{ill|Industrialisation|en|Industrialisation|WD=Q202398|lt=industrialized|1=Industrialisation}} and adopted {{ill|Western culture|en|Western culture|WD=Q478958|lt=Western ideas|1=Western culture}} and production methods.

== Foreign influence ==
In 1853, {{ill|Commodore (United States)|en|Commodore (United States)|WD=Q844242|lt=Commodore|1=Commodore (United States)}} {{ill|Matthew C. Perry|en|Matthew C. Perry|WD=Q61855|lt=Matthew C. Perry|1=Matthew C. Perry}} arrived in Japan. A year later Perry returned in threatening {{ill|Black Ships|en|Black Ships|WD=Q1136943|lt=large warships|1=Black Ships}} with the aspiration of concluding a treaty that would open up Japanese ports for trade.<ref>Hunt, Lynn, Thomas R. Martin, Barbara H. Rosenwein, R. Po-chia Hsia et al. ''The Making of the West, Peoples and Cultures''. Vol. C. 3rd ed. Boston: Bedford/ St. Martin's, 2009. 712–713.</ref> Perry concluded the treaty that would open up two Japanese ports (Shimoda and Hakodate) only for material support, such as firewood, water, food, and coal for U.S. ships. {{ill|Convention of Kanagawa|en|Convention of Kanagawa|WD=Q771451|lt=The Convention of Kanagawa|1=Convention of Kanagawa}} was signed in 1854 and this opened up trade between the United States and Japan. Later, Japan reluctantly expanded its trade deals to France, Britain, the Netherlands and Russia due to American pressure. These treaties signed with Western powers came to be known as [[:en:Unequal treaty|Unequal Treaties]] as Japan lost control over its tariffs while Western powers took control over Japanese lands. In 1858, {{ill|Townsend Harris|en|Townsend Harris|WD=Q610626|lt=Townsend Harris|1=Townsend Harris}}, ambassador to Japan, concluded the treaty, opening Japanese ports to trade. Figures like {{ill|Shimazu Nariakira|en|Shimazu Nariakira|WD=Q1143856|lt=Shimazu Nariakira|1=Shimazu Nariakira}} concluded that "if we take the initiative, we can dominate; if we do not, we will be dominated", leading Japan to "throw open its doors to foreign technology." 

After the humiliation of the Unequal Treaties, the leaders of the Meiji Restoration (as this revolution came to be known), acted in the name of restoring imperial rule to strengthen Japan against the threat of being colonized, bringing to an end the era known as ''{{ill|Sakoku|en|Sakoku|WD=Q332075|lt=Sakoku|1=Sakoku}}''. The word "Meiji" means "enlightened rule" and the goal was to combine "modern advances" with traditional "eastern" values {{Nihongo|2=和魂洋才|4=''Wakonyosai''}}.<ref>Hunt, Lynn, Thomas R. Martin, Barbara H. Rosenwein, R. Po-chia Hsia et al.. ''The Making of the West, Peoples and Cultures''. Vol. C. 3rd ed. Boston: Bedford/ St. Martin's, 2009. 712–713.
* Henry Kissinger ''On China''. 2011 p. 79</ref> The main leaders of this were [[Itō Hirobumi]], {{ill|Matsukata Masayoshi|en|Matsukata Masayoshi|WD=Q714039|lt=Matsukata Masayoshi|1=Matsukata Masayoshi}}, {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|en|Kido Takayoshi|WD=Q696402|lt=Kido Takayoshi|1=Kido Takayoshi}}, {{ill|Itagaki Taisuke|en|Itagaki Taisuke|WD=Q456380|lt=Itagaki Taisuke|1=Itagaki Taisuke}}, {{ill|Yamagata Aritomo|en|Yamagata Aritomo|WD=Q297636|lt=Yamagata Aritomo|1=Yamagata Aritomo}}, {{ill|Mori Arinori|en|Mori Arinori|WD=Q1194472|lt=Mori Arinori|1=Mori Arinori}}, {{ill|Ōkubo Toshimichi|en|Ōkubo Toshimichi|WD=Q356118|lt=Ōkubo Toshimichi|1=Ōkubo Toshimichi}}, and [[Yamaguchi Naoyoshi]].

== Imperial restoration ==
The foundation of the Meiji Restoration was the 1866 {{ill|Satchō Alliance|en|Satchō Alliance|WD=Q700896|lt=Satsuma-Chōshū Alliance|1=Satchō Alliance}} between [[Saigō Takamori]] and {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|en|Kido Takayoshi|WD=Q696402|lt=Kido Takayoshi|1=Kido Takayoshi}}, leaders of the [[Sonnō jōi|reformist]] elements in the {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma|1=Satsuma Domain}} and {{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|WD=Q876267|lt=Chōshū|1=Chōshū Domain}} Domains at the southwestern end of the Japanese archipelago. These two leaders supported the {{ill|Emperor Kōmei|en|Emperor Kōmei|WD=Q299179|lt=Emperor Kōmei|1=Emperor Kōmei}} (Emperor Meiji's father) and were brought together by {{ill|Sakamoto Ryōma|en|Sakamoto Ryōma|WD=Q378450|lt=Sakamoto Ryōma|1=Sakamoto Ryōma}} for the purpose of challenging the ruling [[Tokugawa shogunate]] (''bakufu'') and restoring the Emperor to power. After Kōmei's death on 30 January 1867, Meiji ascended the throne on February{{nbsp}}3. This period also saw Japan change from being a feudal society to having a centralized nation and left the Japanese with a lingering influence of {{ill|Modernity|en|Modernity|WD=Q11084414|lt=Modernity|1=Modernity}}.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Meiji Restoration and Modernization|url=http://afe.easia.columbia.edu/special/japan_1750_meiji.htm|website=Asia for Educators, Columbia University|publisher=Columbia University|access-date=7 May 2018}}</ref>

In the same year, the {{ill|Koban (coin)|en|Koban (coin)|WD=Q43940|lt=koban|1=Koban (coin)}} was discontinued as a form of currency.

== End of the Tokugawa shogunate ==
{{Main|Bakumatsu}}
[[File:Taisehokan.jpg|thumb|[[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]] informs officials of his decision at [[Nijo Castle|Nijō-jō]] in 1867.]]
The Tokugawa government had been founded in the 17th century and initially focused on reestablishing order in social, political and international affairs after a century of warfare. The political structure, established by {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} and solidified under his two immediate successors, his son {{ill|Tokugawa Hidetada|en|Tokugawa Hidetada|WD=Q314464|lt=Tokugawa Hidetada|1=Tokugawa Hidetada}} (who ruled from 1616 to 1623) and grandson {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|en|Tokugawa Iemitsu|WD=Q314481|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu|1=Tokugawa Iemitsu}} (1623–51), bound all [[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s to the shogunate and limited any individual daimyō from acquiring too much land or power.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tokugawa Period and Meiji Restoration |url=http://www.history.com/topics/meiji-restoration|publisher=History.com|access-date=2 March 2018}}</ref> The Tokugawa shogunate came to its official end on 9{{nbsp}}November 1867, when [[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]], the 15th Tokugawa ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'', "put his prerogatives at the Emperor's disposal" and resigned 10 days later.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.britannica.com/event/Meiji-Restoration|title=Meiji Restoration {{!}} Definition, History, & Facts|work=Encyclopedia Britannica|access-date=21 August 2017}}</ref> This was effectively the "restoration" (''Taisei Hōkan'') of imperial rule – although Yoshinobu still had significant influence and it was not until January{{nbsp}}3, the following year, with the young Emperor's edict, that the restoration fully occurred.<ref>"One can date the 'restoration' of imperial rule from the edict of 3{{nbsp}}January 1868." Jansen (2000), p. 334.</ref> On 3 January 1868, the Emperor stripped Yoshinobu of all power and made a formal declaration of the restoration of his power:

{{blockquote|The Emperor of Japan announces to the sovereigns of all foreign countries and to their subjects that permission has been granted to the ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'' Tokugawa Yoshinobu to return the governing power in accordance with his own request. We shall henceforward exercise supreme authority in all the internal and external affairs of the country. Consequently, the title of Emperor must be substituted for that of {{ill|Taikun|en|Taikun|WD=Q1116792|lt=Taikun|1=Taikun}}, in which the treaties have been made. Officers are being appointed by us to the conduct of foreign affairs. It is desirable that the representatives of the treaty powers recognize this announcement.|[[Mutsuhito]], January 3, 1868<ref>Quoted and translated in ''A Diplomat In Japan'', [[:en:Sir Ernest Satow|Sir Ernest Satow]], p. 353, {{ISBN|978-1-933330-16-7}}</ref>}}

Shortly thereafter in January 1868, the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}} started with the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}} in which Chōshū and {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma|1=Satsuma Domain}}'s forces defeated the ex-''shōgun''{{'}}s army. All Tokugawa lands were seized and placed under "imperial control", thus placing them under the prerogative of the new {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Meiji government|1=Government of Meiji Japan}}. With {{ill|Fuhanken sanchisei|en|Fuhanken sanchisei|WD=Q11486110|lt=Fuhanken sanchisei|1=Fuhanken sanchisei}}, the areas were split into three types: {{nihongo|urban {{ill|Prefecture|en|Prefecture|WD=Q515716|lt=Prefecture|1=Prefecture}}s|府|fu}}, {{nihongo|rural prefectures|県|ken}} and the already existing domains.

[[Image:Emperor Receives Foreign Ministers by Hiroshima Kōho (Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery).jpg|thumb|Emperor Meiji receives Dutch Minister-Resident Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek in 1868.]]

On March 23 the Dutch Minister-Resident {{ill|Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek|en|Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek|WD=Q935763|lt=Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek|1=Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek}} and the French Minister-Resident {{ill|Léon Roches|en|Léon Roches|WD=Q972846|lt=Léon Roches|1=Léon Roches}} were the first European envoys ever to receive a personal audience with Meiji in Edo (Tokyo).<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=3YQpz9v8TjQC&dq=Dirk+de+Graeff+van+Polsbroek+meiji&pg=PA133 Emperor of Japan: Meiji and his world, 1852–1912, p 133. Donald Keene]</ref><ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=fyfayVVWBmYC&dq=dirk+de+graeff+van+polsbroek&pg=PA90 The last Samurai: japanische Geschichtsdarstellung im populären Kinofilm, pp 90–91. Daniel Scherer (2009)]</ref> This audience laid the foundation for (modern) Dutch diplomacy in Japan.<ref name="From Dejima to Tokyo">{{Cite web |url=https://www.dejima-tokyo.com/articles/54/Dirk-de-Graeff-van-Polsbroek |title=From Dejima to Tokyo. Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek (This study is the first complete history of Dutch diplomatic locations in Japan. It has been commissioned by the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Tokyo) |access-date=17 March 2023 |archive-date=8 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230308142434/https://www.dejima-tokyo.com/articles/54/Dirk-de-Graeff-van-Polsbroek |url-status=dead }}</ref> Subsequently, De Graeff van Polsbroek assisted the emperor and the government in their negotiations with representatives of the major European powers.<ref name="geheugen">[http://www.geheugenvannederland.nl/?/nl/items/KONB11:s3628-03-p01f4/&p=1&i=9&st=de%20graeff&sc=(%27de%20graeff%27%20*)%20and%20(type%20any%20%27image%20video%20audio%20text%27)/&wst=de%20graeff ''Het geheugen van Nederland'']</ref><ref name="From Dejima to Tokyo"/>

In 1869, the ''daimyōs'' of the {{ill|Tosa Domain|en|Tosa Domain|WD=Q1189704|lt=Tosa|1=Tosa Domain}}, [[:en:Hizen Domain|Hizen]], Satsuma and {{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|WD=Q876267|lt=Chōshū Domain|1=Chōshū Domain}}s, who were pushing most fiercely against the shogunate, were persuaded to "return their domains to the Emperor". Other daimyō were subsequently persuaded to do so, thus creating a central government in Japan which exercised direct power through the entire "realm".{{ref|b}}

Some shogunate forces escaped to [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]], where they attempted to set up a breakaway {{ill|Republic of Ezo|en|Republic of Ezo|WD=Q714006|lt=Republic of Ezo|1=Republic of Ezo}}; however, forces loyal to the Emperor ended this attempt in May 1869 with the {{ill|Battle of Hakodate|en|Battle of Hakodate|WD=Q716562|lt=Battle of Hakodate|1=Battle of Hakodate}} in Hokkaidō. The defeat of the armies of the former ''shōgun'' (led by {{ill|Enomoto Takeaki|en|Enomoto Takeaki|WD=Q532959|lt=Enomoto Takeaki|1=Enomoto Takeaki}} and {{ill|Hijikata Toshizō|en|Hijikata Toshizō|WD=Q701182|lt=Hijikata Toshizō|1=Hijikata Toshizō}}) marked the final end of the Tokugawa shogunate, with the Emperor's power fully restored.{{Citation needed|date=August 2017}}

Finally, by 1872, the ''daimyōs'', past and present, were summoned before the Emperor, where it was declared that {{ill|Abolition of the han system|en|Abolition of the han system|WD=Q331905|lt=all domains were now to be returned to the Emperor|1=Abolition of the han system}}. The roughly 280 domains were turned into 72 prefectures, each under the control of a state-appointed governor. If the ''daimyōs'' peacefully complied, they were given a prominent voice in the new Meiji government.<ref>[[:en:David "Race" Bannon|David "Race" Bannon]], "Redefining Traditional Feudal Ethics in Japan during the Meiji Restoration," Asian Pacific Quarterly, Vol. 26, No. 1 (1994): 27–35.</ref> Later, their debts and payments of samurai stipends were either taxed heavily or turned into bonds which resulted in a large loss of wealth among former samurai.<ref name="polsy"/>

== Military reform ==
{{Main|Meiji period|Government of Meiji Japan|Meiji Constitution|Abolition of the han system}}

Emperor Meiji announced in his 1868 Charter Oath that "Knowledge shall be sought all over the world, and thereby the foundations of imperial rule shall be strengthened."<ref name="China p.79">Henry Kissinger On China. 2011 p. 79</ref>

Under the leadership of {{ill|Mori Arinori|en|Mori Arinori|WD=Q1194472|lt=Mori Arinori|1=Mori Arinori}}, a group of prominent Japanese intellectuals went on to form the {{ill|Meirokusha|en|Meirokusha|WD=Q1783546|lt=Meiji Six Society|1=Meirokusha}} in 1873 to continue to "promote civilization and enlightenment" through modern ethics and ideas. However, during the restoration, political power simply moved from the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] to an {{ill|Oligarchy|en|Oligarchy|WD=Q79751|lt=Oligarchy|1=Oligarchy}} consisting of these leaders, mostly from {{ill|Satsuma Province|en|Satsuma Province|WD=Q667475|lt=Satsuma Province|1=Satsuma Province}} ({{ill|Ōkubo Toshimichi|en|Ōkubo Toshimichi|WD=Q356118|lt=Ōkubo Toshimichi|1=Ōkubo Toshimichi}} and [[Saigō Takamori]]), and [[:en:Chōshū Province|Chōshū Province]] ([[Itō Hirobumi]], {{ill|Yamagata Aritomo|en|Yamagata Aritomo|WD=Q297636|lt=Yamagata Aritomo|1=Yamagata Aritomo}}, and Kido Takayoshi). This reflected their belief in the more traditional practice of imperial rule, whereby the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor of Japan|1=Emperor of Japan}} serves solely as the spiritual authority of the nation and his ministers govern the nation in his name.{{Citation needed|date=August 2017}}

The {{ill|Meiji oligarchy|en|Meiji oligarchy|WD=Q1150742|lt=Meiji oligarchy|1=Meiji oligarchy}} that formed the government under the rule of the Emperor first introduced measures to consolidate their power against the remnants of the Edo period government, the shogunate, ''daimyōs'', and the {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} class.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Federal Research Division |title=Japan: A Country Study |date=1992 |publisher=Library of Congress |pages=38}}</ref>

[[File:Hoheikosho-at-Koishikawa-Arsenal-c1920.png|thumb|The {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}} {{ill|Koishikawa Arsenal|en|Koishikawa Arsenal|WD=Q6426349|lt=Koishikawa Arsenal|1=Koishikawa Arsenal}} was established in 1871.]]
Throughout Japan at the time, the samurai numbered 1.9 million. For comparison, this was more than 10 times the size of the French privileged class before the 1789 {{ill|French Revolution|en|French Revolution|WD=Q6534|lt=French Revolution|1=French Revolution}}. Moreover, the samurai in Japan were not merely the lords, but also their higher retainers—people who actually worked. With each samurai being paid fixed stipends, their upkeep presented a tremendous financial burden, which may have prompted the oligarchs to action.

Whatever their true intentions, the oligarchs embarked on another slow and deliberate process to abolish the samurai class. First, in 1873, it was announced that the samurai stipends were to be taxed on a rolling basis. Later, in 1874, the samurai were given the option to convert their stipends into {{ill|Government bond|en|Government bond|WD=Q2324820|lt=Government bond|1=Government bond}}s. Finally, in 1876, this commutation was made compulsory.{{Citation needed|date=August 2017}}

To reform the military, the government instituted nationwide conscription in 1873, mandating that every male would serve for four years in the armed forces upon turning 21 years old, followed by three more years in the reserves. One of the primary differences between the samurai and peasant classes was the [[:en:Right to bear arms|Right to bear arms]]; this ancient privilege was suddenly extended to every male in the nation. Furthermore, samurai were no longer allowed to walk about town bearing a sword or weapon to show their status.

This led to a series of riots from disgruntled samurai. One of the major riots was the one led by Saigō Takamori, the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|en|Satsuma Rebellion|WD=Q714820|lt=Satsuma Rebellion|1=Satsuma Rebellion}}, which eventually turned into a civil war. This rebellion was, however, put down swiftly by the newly formed {{ill|Imperial Japanese Army|en|Imperial Japanese Army|WD=Q276535|lt=Imperial Japanese Army|1=Imperial Japanese Army}}, trained in Western tactics and weapons, even though the core of the new army was the Tokyo police force, which was largely composed of former samurai. This sent a strong message to the dissenting samurai that their time was indeed over. There were fewer subsequent samurai uprisings and the distinction became all but a name as the samurai joined the new society. The ideal of samurai military spirit lived on in romanticized form and was often used as propaganda during the early 20th-century wars of the {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|WD=Q188712|lt=Empire of Japan|1=Empire of Japan}}.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wert |first1=Michael |title=Samurai: A Concise History |date=26 September 2019 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190932947 |pages=108–109 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eguXDwAAQBAJ&q=samurai+propaganda&pg=PA109 |access-date=7 April 2021}}</ref>

However, it is equally true that the majority of samurai were content despite having their status abolished. Many found employment in the government bureaucracy, which resembled an elite class in its own right. The samurai, being better educated than most of the population, became teachers, gun makers, government officials, and/or military officers. While the formal title of samurai was abolished, the elitist spirit that characterized the samurai class lived on.

The oligarchs also embarked on a series of {{ill|Land Tax Reform (Japan 1873)|en|Land Tax Reform (Japan 1873)|WD=Q3049252|lt=land reforms|1=Land Tax Reform}}. In particular, they legitimized the tenancy system which had been going on during the Tokugawa period. Despite the {{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'s best efforts to freeze the four classes of society in place, during their rule villagers had begun to lease land out to other farmers, becoming rich in the process. This greatly disrupted the clearly defined class system which the bakufu had envisaged, partly leading to their eventual downfall.{{Citation needed|date=August 2017}}

The military of Japan, strengthened by nationwide conscription and emboldened by military success in both the {{ill|First Sino-Japanese War|en|First Sino-Japanese War|WD=Q178687|lt=Sino-Japanese War|1=First Sino-Japanese War}} and the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|en|Russo-Japanese War|WD=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War|1=Russo-Japanese War}}, began to view themselves as a growing world power.

== Centralization ==
[[File:The_New_fighting_the_Old_in_early_Meiji_Japan_circa_1870.jpg|thumb|Allegory of the New fighting the Old, in early Japan Meiji, around 1870]]
Besides drastic changes to the social structure of Japan, in an attempt to create a strong centralized state defining its national identity, the government established a dominant national dialect, called {{Nihongo|"standard language"|標準語|[[:en:Hyōjungo|Hyōjungo]]}}, that replaced local and regional dialects and was based on the patterns of Tokyo's samurai classes. This dialect eventually became the norm in the realms of education, media, government, and business.<ref>Bestor, Theodore C. "Japan." Countries and Their Cultures. Eds. Melvin
Ember and Carol Ember. Vol. 2. New York: Macmillan Reference USA, 2001. 1140–1158. 4 vols. Gale Virtual Reference Library. Gale. Pepperdine University SCELC. 23 November 2009 [http://find.galegroup.com.lib.pepperdine.edu/gvrl/infomark.do?&contentSet=EBKS&type=retrieve&tabID=T001&prodId=GVRL&docId=CX3401700121&source=gale&userGroupName=pepp12906&version=1.0].
</ref>

The Meiji Restoration, and the resultant modernization of Japan, also influenced Japanese self-identity with respect to its Asian neighbours, as Japan became the first Asian state to modernize based on the Western model, replacing the traditional Confucian hierarchical order that had persisted previously under a dominant China with one based on modernity.<ref>{{Cite journal |first=Chih-yu |last=Shih |jstor=23462195 |title=A Rising Unknown: Rediscovering China in Japan's East Asia |date=Spring 2011 |issue=1 |volume=11 |journal=China Review|publisher=Chinese University Press |page=2 }}</ref>
Adopting {{ill|Age of Enlightenment|en|Age of Enlightenment|WD=Q12539|lt=enlightenment|1=Age of Enlightenment}} ideals of popular education, the Japanese government established a national system of public schools.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://afe.easia.columbia.edu/special/japan_1750_meiji.htm|title=The Meiji Restoration and Modernization {{!}} Asia for Educators {{!}} Columbia University|website=afe.easia.columbia.edu|access-date=21 May 2019}}</ref> These free schools taught students reading, writing, and mathematics. Students also attended courses in "moral training" which reinforced their duty to the Emperor and to the Japanese state. By the end of the Meiji period, attendance in public schools was widespread, increasing the availability of skilled workers and contributing to the [[Economic history of Japan#Meiji_era_(1868–1912)|industrial growth of Japan]].

The opening up of Japan not only consisted of the ports being opened for trade, but also began the process of merging members of the different societies together. Examples of this include western teachers and advisors immigrating to Japan and also Japanese nationals moving to western countries for education purposes. All these things in turn played a part in expanding the people of Japan's knowledge on western customs, technology and institutions. Many people believed it was essential for Japan to acquire western "spirit" in order to become a great nation with strong trade routes and military strength.

=== Industrial growth ===
The Meiji Restoration accelerated the [[:en:Industrialization|Industrialization]] process in Japan, which led to its rise as a military power by the year 1895, under the slogan of {{Nihongo|"Enrich the country, strengthen the military"|富国強兵|{{ill|Fukoku kyōhei|en|Fukoku kyōhei|WD=Q707219|lt=Fukoku kyōhei|1=Fukoku kyōhei}}}}.

During the Meiji period, powers such as Europe and the United States helped transform Japan and made them realize a change needed to take place. Some leaders went out to foreign lands and used the knowledge and government writings to help shape and form a more influential government within their walls that allowed for things such as production. Despite the help Japan received from other powers, one of the key factors in Japan's industrializing success was its relative lack of resources, which made it unattractive to Western imperialism.<ref>{{Cite book|title=World Resources and Industries|last=Zimmermann|first=Erich W.|publisher=Harper & Row|year=1951|location=New York|pages=462, 525, 718}}</ref> The farmer and the samurai classification were the base and soon the problem of why there was a limit of growth within the nation's industrial work. The government sent officials such as the samurai to monitor the work that was being done. Because of Japan's leaders taking control and adapting Western techniques it has remained one of the world's largest industrial nations.

The rapid industrialization and modernization of Japan both allowed and required a massive increase in production and infrastructure. Japan built industries such as shipyards, iron smelters, and spinning mills, which were then sold to well-connected entrepreneurs. Consequently, domestic companies became consumers of Western technology and applied it to produce items that would be sold cheaply in the international market. With this, industrial zones grew enormously, and there was a massive migration to industrializing centers from the countryside. Industrialization additionally went hand in hand with the development of a national railway system and modern communications.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yamamura |first1=Kozo |title=Success Illgotten? The Role of Meiji Militarism in Japan's Technological Progress |journal=[[The Journal of Economic History]] |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |volume=37 |number=1 |date=1977 |pages=113–135 |doi=10.1017/S0022050700096777 |jstor = 2119450|s2cid=154563371 }}</ref>

===Destruction of cultural heritage===
The majority of {{ill|Japanese castle|en|Japanese castle|WD=Q92026|lt=Japanese castle|1=Japanese castle}}s were [[Japanese castle#Meiji Restoration|partially or completely dismantled]] in the late 19th century in the Meiji restoration by the national government. Since the feudal system was abolished and the fiefs (''han'') theoretically reverting to the emperor, the national government saw no further use for the upkeep of these now obsolete castles. The military was modernized and some parts of the castles were converted into modern military facilities with barracks and parade grounds, such as {{ill|Hiroshima Castle|en|Hiroshima Castle|WD=Q41977|lt=Hiroshima Castle|1=Hiroshima Castle}}. Others were handed over to the civilian authorities to build their new administrative structures.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2296.html |title= Japanese castles History of Castles |date=4 September 2021 |website= Japan Guide}}</ref> Some however were explicitly saved from destruction by interventions from various persons and parties such as politicians, government and military officials, experts, historians, and locals who feared a loss of their cultural heritage. In the case of {{ill|Hikone Castle|en|Hikone Castle|WD=Q1012374|lt=Hikone Castle|1=Hikone Castle}}, even though the government ordered its dismantling, it was saved by orders from the emperor himself. [[Nagoya Castle]] and [[Nijo Castle]], due to their historical and cultural importance and sheer size and strategic locations, both became official imperial detached palaces, before they were turned over to the local authorities in the 1930s. Others such as [[Himeji Castle]] survived by luck.

During the Meiji restoration's [[Shinbutsu bunri]], tens of thousands of Japanese Buddhist religious idols and temples were smashed and destroyed.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://jref.com/articles/shinbutsu-bunri-the-separation-of-shinto-and-buddhism.468/ |title=Shinbutsu bunri – the separation of Shinto and Buddhism |last= |first= |date=11 July 2019 |website=Japan Reference |publisher= |access-date= |quote=}}</ref> Japan then closed and shut down tens of thousands of traditional old Shinto shrines in the [[Shrine Consolidation Policy]] and the Meiji government built the new modern [[List of the Fifteen Shrines of the Kenmu Restoration|15 shrines of the Kenmu restoration]] as a political move to link the Meiji restoration to the Kenmu restoration for their new {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} cult.

===Outlawing of traditional practices===
In the {{ill|Blood tax riots|en|Blood tax riots|WD=Q11625961|lt=Blood tax riots|1=Blood tax riots}}, the Meiji government put down revolts by Japanese samurai angry that the traditional {{ill|Untouchability|en|Untouchability|WD=Q3216180|lt=untouchable|1=Untouchability}} status of {{ill|Burakumin|en|Burakumin|WD=Q548787|lt=Burakumin|1=Burakumin}} was legally revoked.

Under the Meiji Restoration, the practices of the samurai classes, deemed feudal and unsuitable for modern times following the end of {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Sakoku|en|Sakoku|WD=Q332075|lt=Sakoku|1=Sakoku}}}} in 1853, resulted in a number of edicts intended to 'modernise' the appearance of upper class Japanese men. With the Dampatsurei Edict of 1871 issued by {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} during the early [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], men of the samurai classes were forced to cut their hair short, effectively abandoning the {{ill|Chonmage|en|Chonmage|WD=Q137592|lt=Chonmage|1=Chonmage}} ({{transliteration|ja|chonmage}}) hairstyle.<ref name="kanban">{{cite book |last=Scott Pate |first=Alan |title=Kanban: Traditional Shop Signs of Japan |date=2017 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a4ofDgAAQBAJ&dq=Dampatsurei+Edict&pg=PA149 
|location=New Jersey |publisher=Princeton University Press |quote=In 1871 the Dampatsurei edict forced all samurai to cut off their topknots, a traditional source of identity and pride. |isbn=978-0691176475}}</ref>{{rp|149}}

During the Meiji Restoration, the practice of cremation and Buddhism were condemned and the Japanese government tried to ban cremation but were unsuccessful, then tried to limit it in urban areas. The Japanese government reversed its ban on cremation and pro-cremation Japanese adopted western European arguments on how cremation was good for limiting disease spread, so the Japanese government lifted their attempted ban in May 1875 and promoted cremation for diseased people in 1897.<ref>{{cite news |last=Hiatt   |first=Anna  |date=September 9, 2015 |title= The History of Cremation in Japan |url=https://daily.jstor.org/history-japan-cremation/ |work=Jstor Daily |location= |access-date=}}</ref>

== Use of foreign specialists==
{{main|Foreign government advisors in Meiji Japan}}
Even before the Meiji Restoration, the [[:en:Tokugawa Shogun|Tokugawa Shogun]]ate government hired German diplomat {{ill|Philipp Franz von Siebold|en|Philipp Franz von Siebold|WD=Q77140|lt=Philipp Franz von Siebold|1=Philipp Franz von Siebold}} as diplomatic advisor, Dutch naval engineer Hendrik Hardes for {{ill|Sasebo Naval Arsenal|en|Sasebo Naval Arsenal|WD=Q2754053|lt=Nagasaki Arsenal|1=Sasebo Naval Arsenal}} and {{ill|Willem Huyssen van Kattendijke|en|Willem Huyssen van Kattendijke|WD=Q2547386|lt=Willem Johan Cornelis, Ridder Huijssen van Kattendijke|1=Willem Huyssen van Kattendijke}} for [[Nagasaki Naval Training Center]], French naval engineer [[:en:François Léonce Verny|François Léonce Verny]] for {{ill|Yokosuka Naval Arsenal|en|Yokosuka Naval Arsenal|WD=Q2790777|lt=Yokosuka Naval Arsenal|1=Yokosuka Naval Arsenal}}, and British civil engineer {{ill|Richard Henry Brunton|en|Richard Henry Brunton|WD=Q3430861|lt=Richard Henry Brunton|1=Richard Henry Brunton}}. Most of them were appointed through government approval with two or three years contract, and took their responsibility properly in Japan, except some cases. Then many other foreign specialists were hired.

Despite the value they provided in the modernization of Japan, the Japanese government did not consider it prudent for them to settle in Japan permanently. After their contracts ended, most of them returned to their country except some, like {{ill|Josiah Conder (architect)|en|Josiah Conder (architect)|WD=Q1187770|lt=Josiah Conder|1=Josiah Conder (architect)}} and {{ill|W. K. Burton|en|W. K. Burton|WD=Q702239|lt=W. K. Burton|1=W. K. Burton}}.

== Explanatory notes ==
:1.{{note|a}} Although the political system was consolidated under the Emperor, power was mainly transferred to a group of people, known as the {{ill|Meiji oligarchy|en|Meiji oligarchy|WD=Q1150742|lt=Meiji oligarchy|1=Meiji oligarchy}} (and {{ill|Genrō|en|Genrō|WD=Q254907|lt=Genrō|1=Genrō}}).<ref name="polsy">{{cite book|last1=Gordon|first1=Andrew|title=A Modern History of Japan From Tokugawa Times to the Present.|url=https://archive.org/details/modernhistoryjap00gord|url-access=limited|date=2003|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=New York|isbn=9780198027089|pages=[https://archive.org/details/modernhistoryjap00gord/page/n75 61]–62}}</ref>
:2.{{note|b}}At that time, the new government used the phrase "Itten-banjō" (一天万乗). However, the more generic term [[Tianxia#Japan|天下]] is most commonly used in modern historiography.

{{History of Japan}}

The '''Meiji Restoration''' ({{lang-ja|明治維新|Meiji Ishin}}), referred to at the time as the {{Nihongo|'''Honorable Restoration'''|御維新|Goisshin}}, and also known as the '''Meiji Renovation''', '''Revolution''', '''Regeneration''', '''Reform''', or '''Renewal''', was a political event that restored practical imperial rule to Japan in 1868 under {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}}. Although there were ruling emperors before the Meiji Restoration, the events restored practical abilities and consolidated the political system under the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor of Japan|1=Emperor of Japan}}.{{ref|a}} The goals of the restored government were expressed by the new emperor in the {{ill|Charter Oath|en|Charter Oath|WD=Q702056|lt=Charter Oath|1=Charter Oath}}

The Restoration led to enormous changes in Japan's political and social structure and spanned both the late {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} (often called the {{ill|Bakumatsu|en|Bakumatsu|WD=Q804558|lt=Bakumatsu|1=Bakumatsu}}) and the beginning of the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], during which time Japan rapidly {{ill|Industrialisation|en|Industrialisation|WD=Q202398|lt=industrialized|1=Industrialisation}} and adopted {{ill|Western culture|en|Western culture|WD=Q478958|lt=Western ideas|1=Western culture}} and production methods.

== Foreign influence ==
In 1853, {{ill|Commodore (United States)|en|Commodore (United States)|WD=Q844242|lt=Commodore|1=Commodore (United States)}} {{ill|Matthew C. Perry|en|Matthew C. Perry|WD=Q61855|lt=Matthew C. Perry|1=Matthew C. Perry}} arrived in Japan. A year later Perry returned in threatening {{ill|Black Ships|en|Black Ships|WD=Q1136943|lt=large warships|1=Black Ships}} with the aspiration of concluding a treaty that would open up Japanese ports for trade.<ref>Hunt, Lynn, Thomas R. Martin, Barbara H. Rosenwein, R. Po-chia Hsia et al. ''The Making of the West, Peoples and Cultures''. Vol. C. 3rd ed. Boston: Bedford/ St. Martin's, 2009. 712–713.</ref> Perry concluded the treaty that would open up two Japanese ports (Shimoda and Hakodate) only for material support, such as firewood, water, food, and coal for U.S. ships. {{ill|Convention of Kanagawa|en|Convention of Kanagawa|WD=Q771451|lt=The Convention of Kanagawa|1=Convention of Kanagawa}} was signed in 1854 and this opened up trade between the United States and Japan. Later, Japan reluctantly expanded its trade deals to France, Britain, the Netherlands and Russia due to American pressure. These treaties signed with Western powers came to be known as [[:en:Unequal treaty|Unequal Treaties]] as Japan lost control over its tariffs while Western powers took control over Japanese lands. In 1858, {{ill|Townsend Harris|en|Townsend Harris|WD=Q610626|lt=Townsend Harris|1=Townsend Harris}}, ambassador to Japan, concluded the treaty, opening Japanese ports to trade. Figures like {{ill|Shimazu Nariakira|en|Shimazu Nariakira|WD=Q1143856|lt=Shimazu Nariakira|1=Shimazu Nariakira}} concluded that "if we take the initiative, we can dominate; if we do not, we will be dominated", leading Japan to "throw open its doors to foreign technology." 

After the humiliation of the Unequal Treaties, the leaders of the Meiji Restoration (as this revolution came to be known), acted in the name of restoring imperial rule to strengthen Japan against the threat of being colonized, bringing to an end the era known as ''{{ill|Sakoku|en|Sakoku|WD=Q332075|lt=Sakoku|1=Sakoku}}''. The word "Meiji" means "enlightened rule" and the goal was to combine "modern advances" with traditional "eastern" values {{Nihongo|2=和魂洋才|4=''Wakonyosai''}}.<ref>Hunt, Lynn, Thomas R. Martin, Barbara H. Rosenwein, R. Po-chia Hsia et al.. ''The Making of the West, Peoples and Cultures''. Vol. C. 3rd ed. Boston: Bedford/ St. Martin's, 2009. 712–713.
* Henry Kissinger ''On China''. 2011 p. 79</ref> The main leaders of this were [[Itō Hirobumi]], {{ill|Matsukata Masayoshi|en|Matsukata Masayoshi|WD=Q714039|lt=Matsukata Masayoshi|1=Matsukata Masayoshi}}, {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|en|Kido Takayoshi|WD=Q696402|lt=Kido Takayoshi|1=Kido Takayoshi}}, {{ill|Itagaki Taisuke|en|Itagaki Taisuke|WD=Q456380|lt=Itagaki Taisuke|1=Itagaki Taisuke}}, {{ill|Yamagata Aritomo|en|Yamagata Aritomo|WD=Q297636|lt=Yamagata Aritomo|1=Yamagata Aritomo}}, {{ill|Mori Arinori|en|Mori Arinori|WD=Q1194472|lt=Mori Arinori|1=Mori Arinori}}, {{ill|Ōkubo Toshimichi|en|Ōkubo Toshimichi|WD=Q356118|lt=Ōkubo Toshimichi|1=Ōkubo Toshimichi}}, and [[Yamaguchi Naoyoshi]].

== Imperial restoration ==
The foundation of the Meiji Restoration was the 1866 {{ill|Satchō Alliance|en|Satchō Alliance|WD=Q700896|lt=Satsuma-Chōshū Alliance|1=Satchō Alliance}} between [[Saigō Takamori]] and {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|en|Kido Takayoshi|WD=Q696402|lt=Kido Takayoshi|1=Kido Takayoshi}}, leaders of the [[Sonnō jōi|reformist]] elements in the {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma|1=Satsuma Domain}} and {{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|WD=Q876267|lt=Chōshū|1=Chōshū Domain}} Domains at the southwestern end of the Japanese archipelago. These two leaders supported the {{ill|Emperor Kōmei|en|Emperor Kōmei|WD=Q299179|lt=Emperor Kōmei|1=Emperor Kōmei}} (Emperor Meiji's father) and were brought together by {{ill|Sakamoto Ryōma|en|Sakamoto Ryōma|WD=Q378450|lt=Sakamoto Ryōma|1=Sakamoto Ryōma}} for the purpose of challenging the ruling [[Tokugawa shogunate]] (''bakufu'') and restoring the Emperor to power. After Kōmei's death on 30 January 1867, Meiji ascended the throne on February{{nbsp}}3. This period also saw Japan change from being a feudal society to having a centralized nation and left the Japanese with a lingering influence of {{ill|Modernity|en|Modernity|WD=Q11084414|lt=Modernity|1=Modernity}}.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Meiji Restoration and Modernization|url=http://afe.easia.columbia.edu/special/japan_1750_meiji.htm|website=Asia for Educators, Columbia University|publisher=Columbia University|access-date=7 May 2018}}</ref>

In the same year, the {{ill|Koban (coin)|en|Koban (coin)|WD=Q43940|lt=koban|1=Koban (coin)}} was discontinued as a form of currency.

== End of the Tokugawa shogunate ==
{{Main|Bakumatsu}}
[[File:Taisehokan.jpg|thumb|[[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]] informs officials of his decision at [[Nijo Castle|Nijō-jō]] in 1867.]]
The Tokugawa government had been founded in the 17th century and initially focused on reestablishing order in social, political and international affairs after a century of warfare. The political structure, established by {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|en|Tokugawa Ieyasu|WD=Q171977|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} and solidified under his two immediate successors, his son {{ill|Tokugawa Hidetada|en|Tokugawa Hidetada|WD=Q314464|lt=Tokugawa Hidetada|1=Tokugawa Hidetada}} (who ruled from 1616 to 1623) and grandson {{ill|Tokugawa Iemitsu|en|Tokugawa Iemitsu|WD=Q314481|lt=Tokugawa Iemitsu|1=Tokugawa Iemitsu}} (1623–51), bound all [[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s to the shogunate and limited any individual daimyō from acquiring too much land or power.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tokugawa Period and Meiji Restoration |url=http://www.history.com/topics/meiji-restoration|publisher=History.com|access-date=2 March 2018}}</ref> The Tokugawa shogunate came to its official end on 9{{nbsp}}November 1867, when [[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]], the 15th Tokugawa ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'', "put his prerogatives at the Emperor's disposal" and resigned 10 days later.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.britannica.com/event/Meiji-Restoration|title=Meiji Restoration {{!}} Definition, History, & Facts|work=Encyclopedia Britannica|access-date=21 August 2017}}</ref> This was effectively the "restoration" (''Taisei Hōkan'') of imperial rule – although Yoshinobu still had significant influence and it was not until January{{nbsp}}3, the following year, with the young Emperor's edict, that the restoration fully occurred.<ref>"One can date the 'restoration' of imperial rule from the edict of 3{{nbsp}}January 1868." Jansen (2000), p. 334.</ref> On 3 January 1868, the Emperor stripped Yoshinobu of all power and made a formal declaration of the restoration of his power:

{{blockquote|The Emperor of Japan announces to the sovereigns of all foreign countries and to their subjects that permission has been granted to the ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'' Tokugawa Yoshinobu to return the governing power in accordance with his own request. We shall henceforward exercise supreme authority in all the internal and external affairs of the country. Consequently, the title of Emperor must be substituted for that of {{ill|Taikun|en|Taikun|WD=Q1116792|lt=Taikun|1=Taikun}}, in which the treaties have been made. Officers are being appointed by us to the conduct of foreign affairs. It is desirable that the representatives of the treaty powers recognize this announcement.|[[Mutsuhito]], January 3, 1868<ref>Quoted and translated in ''A Diplomat In Japan'', [[:en:Sir Ernest Satow|Sir Ernest Satow]], p. 353, {{ISBN|978-1-933330-16-7}}</ref>}}

Shortly thereafter in January 1868, the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}} started with the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}} in which Chōshū and {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma|1=Satsuma Domain}}'s forces defeated the ex-''shōgun''{{'}}s army. All Tokugawa lands were seized and placed under "imperial control", thus placing them under the prerogative of the new {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Meiji government|1=Government of Meiji Japan}}. With {{ill|Fuhanken sanchisei|en|Fuhanken sanchisei|WD=Q11486110|lt=Fuhanken sanchisei|1=Fuhanken sanchisei}}, the areas were split into three types: {{nihongo|urban {{ill|Prefecture|en|Prefecture|WD=Q515716|lt=Prefecture|1=Prefecture}}s|府|fu}}, {{nihongo|rural prefectures|県|ken}} and the already existing domains.

[[Image:Emperor Receives Foreign Ministers by Hiroshima Kōho (Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery).jpg|thumb|Emperor Meiji receives Dutch Minister-Resident Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek in 1868.]]

On March 23 the Dutch Minister-Resident {{ill|Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek|en|Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek|WD=Q935763|lt=Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek|1=Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek}} and the French Minister-Resident {{ill|Léon Roches|en|Léon Roches|WD=Q972846|lt=Léon Roches|1=Léon Roches}} were the first European envoys ever to receive a personal audience with Meiji in Edo (Tokyo).<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=3YQpz9v8TjQC&dq=Dirk+de+Graeff+van+Polsbroek+meiji&pg=PA133 Emperor of Japan: Meiji and his world, 1852–1912, p 133. Donald Keene]</ref><ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=fyfayVVWBmYC&dq=dirk+de+graeff+van+polsbroek&pg=PA90 The last Samurai: japanische Geschichtsdarstellung im populären Kinofilm, pp 90–91. Daniel Scherer (2009)]</ref> This audience laid the foundation for (modern) Dutch diplomacy in Japan.<ref name="From Dejima to Tokyo">{{Cite web |url=https://www.dejima-tokyo.com/articles/54/Dirk-de-Graeff-van-Polsbroek |title=From Dejima to Tokyo. Dirk de Graeff van Polsbroek (This study is the first complete history of Dutch diplomatic locations in Japan. It has been commissioned by the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Tokyo) |access-date=17 March 2023 |archive-date=8 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230308142434/https://www.dejima-tokyo.com/articles/54/Dirk-de-Graeff-van-Polsbroek |url-status=dead }}</ref> Subsequently, De Graeff van Polsbroek assisted the emperor and the government in their negotiations with representatives of the major European powers.<ref name="geheugen">[http://www.geheugenvannederland.nl/?/nl/items/KONB11:s3628-03-p01f4/&p=1&i=9&st=de%20graeff&sc=(%27de%20graeff%27%20*)%20and%20(type%20any%20%27image%20video%20audio%20text%27)/&wst=de%20graeff ''Het geheugen van Nederland'']</ref><ref name="From Dejima to Tokyo"/>

In 1869, the ''daimyōs'' of the {{ill|Tosa Domain|en|Tosa Domain|WD=Q1189704|lt=Tosa|1=Tosa Domain}}, [[:en:Hizen Domain|Hizen]], Satsuma and {{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|WD=Q876267|lt=Chōshū Domain|1=Chōshū Domain}}s, who were pushing most fiercely against the shogunate, were persuaded to "return their domains to the Emperor". Other daimyō were subsequently persuaded to do so, thus creating a central government in Japan which exercised direct power through the entire "realm".{{ref|b}}

Some shogunate forces escaped to [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]], where they attempted to set up a breakaway {{ill|Republic of Ezo|en|Republic of Ezo|WD=Q714006|lt=Republic of Ezo|1=Republic of Ezo}}; however, forces loyal to the Emperor ended this attempt in May 1869 with the {{ill|Battle of Hakodate|en|Battle of Hakodate|WD=Q716562|lt=Battle of Hakodate|1=Battle of Hakodate}} in Hokkaidō. The defeat of the armies of the former ''shōgun'' (led by {{ill|Enomoto Takeaki|en|Enomoto Takeaki|WD=Q532959|lt=Enomoto Takeaki|1=Enomoto Takeaki}} and {{ill|Hijikata Toshizō|en|Hijikata Toshizō|WD=Q701182|lt=Hijikata Toshizō|1=Hijikata Toshizō}}) marked the final end of the Tokugawa shogunate, with the Emperor's power fully restored.{{Citation needed|date=August 2017}}

Finally, by 1872, the ''daimyōs'', past and present, were summoned before the Emperor, where it was declared that {{ill|Abolition of the han system|en|Abolition of the han system|WD=Q331905|lt=all domains were now to be returned to the Emperor|1=Abolition of the han system}}. The roughly 280 domains were turned into 72 prefectures, each under the control of a state-appointed governor. If the ''daimyōs'' peacefully complied, they were given a prominent voice in the new Meiji government.<ref>[[:en:David "Race" Bannon|David "Race" Bannon]], "Redefining Traditional Feudal Ethics in Japan during the Meiji Restoration," Asian Pacific Quarterly, Vol. 26, No. 1 (1994): 27–35.</ref> Later, their debts and payments of samurai stipends were either taxed heavily or turned into bonds which resulted in a large loss of wealth among former samurai.<ref name="polsy"/>

== Military reform ==
{{Main|Meiji period|Government of Meiji Japan|Meiji Constitution|Abolition of the han system}}

Emperor Meiji announced in his 1868 Charter Oath that "Knowledge shall be sought all over the world, and thereby the foundations of imperial rule shall be strengthened."<ref name="China p.79">Henry Kissinger On China. 2011 p. 79</ref>

Under the leadership of {{ill|Mori Arinori|en|Mori Arinori|WD=Q1194472|lt=Mori Arinori|1=Mori Arinori}}, a group of prominent Japanese intellectuals went on to form the {{ill|Meirokusha|en|Meirokusha|WD=Q1783546|lt=Meiji Six Society|1=Meirokusha}} in 1873 to continue to "promote civilization and enlightenment" through modern ethics and ideas. However, during the restoration, political power simply moved from the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] to an {{ill|Oligarchy|en|Oligarchy|WD=Q79751|lt=Oligarchy|1=Oligarchy}} consisting of these leaders, mostly from {{ill|Satsuma Province|en|Satsuma Province|WD=Q667475|lt=Satsuma Province|1=Satsuma Province}} ({{ill|Ōkubo Toshimichi|en|Ōkubo Toshimichi|WD=Q356118|lt=Ōkubo Toshimichi|1=Ōkubo Toshimichi}} and [[Saigō Takamori]]), and [[:en:Chōshū Province|Chōshū Province]] ([[Itō Hirobumi]], {{ill|Yamagata Aritomo|en|Yamagata Aritomo|WD=Q297636|lt=Yamagata Aritomo|1=Yamagata Aritomo}}, and Kido Takayoshi). This reflected their belief in the more traditional practice of imperial rule, whereby the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor of Japan|1=Emperor of Japan}} serves solely as the spiritual authority of the nation and his ministers govern the nation in his name.{{Citation needed|date=August 2017}}

The {{ill|Meiji oligarchy|en|Meiji oligarchy|WD=Q1150742|lt=Meiji oligarchy|1=Meiji oligarchy}} that formed the government under the rule of the Emperor first introduced measures to consolidate their power against the remnants of the Edo period government, the shogunate, ''daimyōs'', and the {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} class.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Federal Research Division |title=Japan: A Country Study |date=1992 |publisher=Library of Congress |pages=38}}</ref>

[[File:Hoheikosho-at-Koishikawa-Arsenal-c1920.png|thumb|The {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}} {{ill|Koishikawa Arsenal|en|Koishikawa Arsenal|WD=Q6426349|lt=Koishikawa Arsenal|1=Koishikawa Arsenal}} was established in 1871.]]
Throughout Japan at the time, the samurai numbered 1.9 million. For comparison, this was more than 10 times the size of the French privileged class before the 1789 {{ill|French Revolution|en|French Revolution|WD=Q6534|lt=French Revolution|1=French Revolution}}. Moreover, the samurai in Japan were not merely the lords, but also their higher retainers—people who actually worked. With each samurai being paid fixed stipends, their upkeep presented a tremendous financial burden, which may have prompted the oligarchs to action.

Whatever their true intentions, the oligarchs embarked on another slow and deliberate process to abolish the samurai class. First, in 1873, it was announced that the samurai stipends were to be taxed on a rolling basis. Later, in 1874, the samurai were given the option to convert their stipends into {{ill|Government bond|en|Government bond|WD=Q2324820|lt=Government bond|1=Government bond}}s. Finally, in 1876, this commutation was made compulsory.{{Citation needed|date=August 2017}}

To reform the military, the government instituted nationwide conscription in 1873, mandating that every male would serve for four years in the armed forces upon turning 21 years old, followed by three more years in the reserves. One of the primary differences between the samurai and peasant classes was the [[:en:Right to bear arms|Right to bear arms]]; this ancient privilege was suddenly extended to every male in the nation. Furthermore, samurai were no longer allowed to walk about town bearing a sword or weapon to show their status.

This led to a series of riots from disgruntled samurai. One of the major riots was the one led by Saigō Takamori, the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|en|Satsuma Rebellion|WD=Q714820|lt=Satsuma Rebellion|1=Satsuma Rebellion}}, which eventually turned into a civil war. This rebellion was, however, put down swiftly by the newly formed {{ill|Imperial Japanese Army|en|Imperial Japanese Army|WD=Q276535|lt=Imperial Japanese Army|1=Imperial Japanese Army}}, trained in Western tactics and weapons, even though the core of the new army was the Tokyo police force, which was largely composed of former samurai. This sent a strong message to the dissenting samurai that their time was indeed over. There were fewer subsequent samurai uprisings and the distinction became all but a name as the samurai joined the new society. The ideal of samurai military spirit lived on in romanticized form and was often used as propaganda during the early 20th-century wars of the {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|WD=Q188712|lt=Empire of Japan|1=Empire of Japan}}.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wert |first1=Michael |title=Samurai: A Concise History |date=26 September 2019 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190932947 |pages=108–109 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eguXDwAAQBAJ&q=samurai+propaganda&pg=PA109 |access-date=7 April 2021}}</ref>

However, it is equally true that the majority of samurai were content despite having their status abolished. Many found employment in the government bureaucracy, which resembled an elite class in its own right. The samurai, being better educated than most of the population, became teachers, gun makers, government officials, and/or military officers. While the formal title of samurai was abolished, the elitist spirit that characterized the samurai class lived on.

The oligarchs also embarked on a series of {{ill|Land Tax Reform (Japan 1873)|en|Land Tax Reform (Japan 1873)|WD=Q3049252|lt=land reforms|1=Land Tax Reform}}. In particular, they legitimized the tenancy system which had been going on during the Tokugawa period. Despite the {{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}'s best efforts to freeze the four classes of society in place, during their rule villagers had begun to lease land out to other farmers, becoming rich in the process. This greatly disrupted the clearly defined class system which the bakufu had envisaged, partly leading to their eventual downfall.{{Citation needed|date=August 2017}}

The military of Japan, strengthened by nationwide conscription and emboldened by military success in both the {{ill|First Sino-Japanese War|en|First Sino-Japanese War|WD=Q178687|lt=Sino-Japanese War|1=First Sino-Japanese War}} and the {{ill|Russo-Japanese War|en|Russo-Japanese War|WD=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War|1=Russo-Japanese War}}, began to view themselves as a growing world power.

== Centralization ==
[[File:The_New_fighting_the_Old_in_early_Meiji_Japan_circa_1870.jpg|thumb|Allegory of the New fighting the Old, in early Japan Meiji, around 1870]]
Besides drastic changes to the social structure of Japan, in an attempt to create a strong centralized state defining its national identity, the government established a dominant national dialect, called {{Nihongo|"standard language"|標準語|[[:en:Hyōjungo|Hyōjungo]]}}, that replaced local and regional dialects and was based on the patterns of Tokyo's samurai classes. This dialect eventually became the norm in the realms of education, media, government, and business.<ref>Bestor, Theodore C. "Japan." Countries and Their Cultures. Eds. Melvin
Ember and Carol Ember. Vol. 2. New York: Macmillan Reference USA, 2001. 1140–1158. 4 vols. Gale Virtual Reference Library. Gale. Pepperdine University SCELC. 23 November 2009 [http://find.galegroup.com.lib.pepperdine.edu/gvrl/infomark.do?&contentSet=EBKS&type=retrieve&tabID=T001&prodId=GVRL&docId=CX3401700121&source=gale&userGroupName=pepp12906&version=1.0].
</ref>

The Meiji Restoration, and the resultant modernization of Japan, also influenced Japanese self-identity with respect to its Asian neighbours, as Japan became the first Asian state to modernize based on the Western model, replacing the traditional Confucian hierarchical order that had persisted previously under a dominant China with one based on modernity.<ref>{{Cite journal |first=Chih-yu |last=Shih |jstor=23462195 |title=A Rising Unknown: Rediscovering China in Japan's East Asia |date=Spring 2011 |issue=1 |volume=11 |journal=China Review|publisher=Chinese University Press |page=2 }}</ref>
Adopting {{ill|Age of Enlightenment|en|Age of Enlightenment|WD=Q12539|lt=enlightenment|1=Age of Enlightenment}} ideals of popular education, the Japanese government established a national system of public schools.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://afe.easia.columbia.edu/special/japan_1750_meiji.htm|title=The Meiji Restoration and Modernization {{!}} Asia for Educators {{!}} Columbia University|website=afe.easia.columbia.edu|access-date=21 May 2019}}</ref> These free schools taught students reading, writing, and mathematics. Students also attended courses in "moral training" which reinforced their duty to the Emperor and to the Japanese state. By the end of the Meiji period, attendance in public schools was widespread, increasing the availability of skilled workers and contributing to the [[Economic history of Japan#Meiji_era_(1868–1912)|industrial growth of Japan]].

The opening up of Japan not only consisted of the ports being opened for trade, but also began the process of merging members of the different societies together. Examples of this include western teachers and advisors immigrating to Japan and also Japanese nationals moving to western countries for education purposes. All these things in turn played a part in expanding the people of Japan's knowledge on western customs, technology and institutions. Many people believed it was essential for Japan to acquire western "spirit" in order to become a great nation with strong trade routes and military strength.

=== Industrial growth ===
The Meiji Restoration accelerated the [[:en:Industrialization|Industrialization]] process in Japan, which led to its rise as a military power by the year 1895, under the slogan of {{Nihongo|"Enrich the country, strengthen the military"|富国強兵|{{ill|Fukoku kyōhei|en|Fukoku kyōhei|WD=Q707219|lt=Fukoku kyōhei|1=Fukoku kyōhei}}}}.

During the Meiji period, powers such as Europe and the United States helped transform Japan and made them realize a change needed to take place. Some leaders went out to foreign lands and used the knowledge and government writings to help shape and form a more influential government within their walls that allowed for things such as production. Despite the help Japan received from other powers, one of the key factors in Japan's industrializing success was its relative lack of resources, which made it unattractive to Western imperialism.<ref>{{Cite book|title=World Resources and Industries|last=Zimmermann|first=Erich W.|publisher=Harper & Row|year=1951|location=New York|pages=462, 525, 718}}</ref> The farmer and the samurai classification were the base and soon the problem of why there was a limit of growth within the nation's industrial work. The government sent officials such as the samurai to monitor the work that was being done. Because of Japan's leaders taking control and adapting Western techniques it has remained one of the world's largest industrial nations.

The rapid industrialization and modernization of Japan both allowed and required a massive increase in production and infrastructure. Japan built industries such as shipyards, iron smelters, and spinning mills, which were then sold to well-connected entrepreneurs. Consequently, domestic companies became consumers of Western technology and applied it to produce items that would be sold cheaply in the international market. With this, industrial zones grew enormously, and there was a massive migration to industrializing centers from the countryside. Industrialization additionally went hand in hand with the development of a national railway system and modern communications.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yamamura |first1=Kozo |title=Success Illgotten? The Role of Meiji Militarism in Japan's Technological Progress |journal=[[The Journal of Economic History]] |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |volume=37 |number=1 |date=1977 |pages=113–135 |doi=10.1017/S0022050700096777 |jstor = 2119450|s2cid=154563371 }}</ref>

===Destruction of cultural heritage===
The majority of {{ill|Japanese castle|en|Japanese castle|WD=Q92026|lt=Japanese castle|1=Japanese castle}}s were [[Japanese castle#Meiji Restoration|partially or completely dismantled]] in the late 19th century in the Meiji restoration by the national government. Since the feudal system was abolished and the fiefs (''han'') theoretically reverting to the emperor, the national government saw no further use for the upkeep of these now obsolete castles. The military was modernized and some parts of the castles were converted into modern military facilities with barracks and parade grounds, such as {{ill|Hiroshima Castle|en|Hiroshima Castle|WD=Q41977|lt=Hiroshima Castle|1=Hiroshima Castle}}. Others were handed over to the civilian authorities to build their new administrative structures.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.japan-guide.com/e/e2296.html |title= Japanese castles History of Castles |date=4 September 2021 |website= Japan Guide}}</ref> Some however were explicitly saved from destruction by interventions from various persons and parties such as politicians, government and military officials, experts, historians, and locals who feared a loss of their cultural heritage. In the case of {{ill|Hikone Castle|en|Hikone Castle|WD=Q1012374|lt=Hikone Castle|1=Hikone Castle}}, even though the government ordered its dismantling, it was saved by orders from the emperor himself. [[Nagoya Castle]] and [[Nijo Castle]], due to their historical and cultural importance and sheer size and strategic locations, both became official imperial detached palaces, before they were turned over to the local authorities in the 1930s. Others such as [[Himeji Castle]] survived by luck.

During the Meiji restoration's [[Shinbutsu bunri]], tens of thousands of Japanese Buddhist religious idols and temples were smashed and destroyed.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://jref.com/articles/shinbutsu-bunri-the-separation-of-shinto-and-buddhism.468/ |title=Shinbutsu bunri – the separation of Shinto and Buddhism |last= |first= |date=11 July 2019 |website=Japan Reference |publisher= |access-date= |quote=}}</ref> Japan then closed and shut down tens of thousands of traditional old Shinto shrines in the [[Shrine Consolidation Policy]] and the Meiji government built the new modern [[List of the Fifteen Shrines of the Kenmu Restoration|15 shrines of the Kenmu restoration]] as a political move to link the Meiji restoration to the Kenmu restoration for their new {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto|1=State Shinto}} cult.

===Outlawing of traditional practices===
In the {{ill|Blood tax riots|en|Blood tax riots|WD=Q11625961|lt=Blood tax riots|1=Blood tax riots}}, the Meiji government put down revolts by Japanese samurai angry that the traditional {{ill|Untouchability|en|Untouchability|WD=Q3216180|lt=untouchable|1=Untouchability}} status of {{ill|Burakumin|en|Burakumin|WD=Q548787|lt=Burakumin|1=Burakumin}} was legally revoked.

Under the Meiji Restoration, the practices of the samurai classes, deemed feudal and unsuitable for modern times following the end of {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Sakoku|en|Sakoku|WD=Q332075|lt=Sakoku|1=Sakoku}}}} in 1853, resulted in a number of edicts intended to 'modernise' the appearance of upper class Japanese men. With the Dampatsurei Edict of 1871 issued by {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} during the early [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], men of the samurai classes were forced to cut their hair short, effectively abandoning the {{ill|Chonmage|en|Chonmage|WD=Q137592|lt=Chonmage|1=Chonmage}} ({{transliteration|ja|chonmage}}) hairstyle.<ref name="kanban">{{cite book |last=Scott Pate |first=Alan |title=Kanban: Traditional Shop Signs of Japan |date=2017 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a4ofDgAAQBAJ&dq=Dampatsurei+Edict&pg=PA149 
|location=New Jersey |publisher=Princeton University Press |quote=In 1871 the Dampatsurei edict forced all samurai to cut off their topknots, a traditional source of identity and pride. |isbn=978-0691176475}}</ref>{{rp|149}}

During the Meiji Restoration, the practice of cremation and Buddhism were condemned and the Japanese government tried to ban cremation but were unsuccessful, then tried to limit it in urban areas. The Japanese government reversed its ban on cremation and pro-cremation Japanese adopted western European arguments on how cremation was good for limiting disease spread, so the Japanese government lifted their attempted ban in May 1875 and promoted cremation for diseased people in 1897.<ref>{{cite news |last=Hiatt   |first=Anna  |date=September 9, 2015 |title= The History of Cremation in Japan |url=https://daily.jstor.org/history-japan-cremation/ |work=Jstor Daily |location= |access-date=}}</ref>

== Use of foreign specialists==
{{main|Foreign government advisors in Meiji Japan}}
Even before the Meiji Restoration, the [[:en:Tokugawa Shogun|Tokugawa Shogun]]ate government hired German diplomat {{ill|Philipp Franz von Siebold|en|Philipp Franz von Siebold|WD=Q77140|lt=Philipp Franz von Siebold|1=Philipp Franz von Siebold}} as diplomatic advisor, Dutch naval engineer Hendrik Hardes for {{ill|Sasebo Naval Arsenal|en|Sasebo Naval Arsenal|WD=Q2754053|lt=Nagasaki Arsenal|1=Sasebo Naval Arsenal}} and {{ill|Willem Huyssen van Kattendijke|en|Willem Huyssen van Kattendijke|WD=Q2547386|lt=Willem Johan Cornelis, Ridder Huijssen van Kattendijke|1=Willem Huyssen van Kattendijke}} for [[Nagasaki Naval Training Center]], French naval engineer [[:en:François Léonce Verny|François Léonce Verny]] for {{ill|Yokosuka Naval Arsenal|en|Yokosuka Naval Arsenal|WD=Q2790777|lt=Yokosuka Naval Arsenal|1=Yokosuka Naval Arsenal}}, and British civil engineer {{ill|Richard Henry Brunton|en|Richard Henry Brunton|WD=Q3430861|lt=Richard Henry Brunton|1=Richard Henry Brunton}}. Most of them were appointed through government approval with two or three years contract, and took their responsibility properly in Japan, except some cases. Then many other foreign specialists were hired.

Despite the value they provided in the modernization of Japan, the Japanese government did not consider it prudent for them to settle in Japan permanently. After their contracts ended, most of them returned to their country except some, like {{ill|Josiah Conder (architect)|en|Josiah Conder (architect)|WD=Q1187770|lt=Josiah Conder|1=Josiah Conder (architect)}} and {{ill|W. K. Burton|en|W. K. Burton|WD=Q702239|lt=W. K. Burton|1=W. K. Burton}}.

:1.{{note|a}} Although the political system was consolidated under the Emperor, power was mainly transferred to a group of people, known as the {{ill|Meiji oligarchy|en|Meiji oligarchy|WD=Q1150742|lt=Meiji oligarchy|1=Meiji oligarchy}} (and {{ill|Genrō|en|Genrō|WD=Q254907|lt=Genrō|1=Genrō}}).<ref name="polsy">{{cite book|last1=Gordon|first1=Andrew|title=A Modern History of Japan From Tokugawa Times to the Present.|url=https://archive.org/details/modernhistoryjap00gord|url-access=limited|date=2003|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=New York|isbn=9780198027089|pages=[https://archive.org/details/modernhistoryjap00gord/page/n75 61]–62}}</ref>
:2.{{note|b}}At that time, the new government used the phrase "Itten-banjō" (一天万乗). However, the more generic term [[Tianxia#Japan|天下]] is most commonly used in modern historiography.
